Preface

Stability is a universal concept which we experience in our everyday lives. When
sitting in a airliner bound to a remote destination, one particularly dislike the
trembling, shaking and the other uncomfortable behaviors that result from the
encounter with a perturbation such as a sudden strong wind. Under the action
of the perturbation the plane can start to oscillate about its main axis. But as
soon as the perturbation is left behind, the undesirable oscillations are damped
over time and the flight quickly becomes enjoyable again. Such a behavior is
typical of a dynamically stable airliner. Had the plane not been stable, it would
not have returned to its initial equilibrium forcing the pilot to compensate for
the oscillations. Many additional examples could be given and all of them
would emphasize the central place held by stability in the control field.
     The question of finding the nearest stable system appears to be a challenging
problem for the research community where one sometimes faces unstable models
created from the perturbed data of a stable system. Though the question has
been mentioned frequently in the literature, the absence of a reference which
solves the problem motivates our research of dedicated algorithms. Very few
existing methods are available to solve the problem due to the nonsmooth,
nonconvex nature of the stable set. The importance and the complexity of the
problem nonetheless calls for additional methods that are specifically designed
to tackle the nearest stable system problem.
     The goals that we want to achieve are, broadly, the development of new and
efficient optimization methods for solving the nearest stable system problem.
Many different approaches can be considered and each of them can potentially
lead to an innovative way of solving the problem. We will base our work
on the well-established theory developed by the optimization community, and
more specifically by the convex optimization community, and favor an approach
where the structure of the different formulations is fully exploited.
     Under some specific conditions closed form solutions for the nearest stable
system are available. This is the case for example when additional constraints
on the shape of the solution are formulated. But a closed form solution is other-
wise illusory since the stable set is nonconvex and even checking the optimality
of a solution once it is computed is challenging. Therefore, numerical methods
that are able to find a nearest stable matrix locally are our only available pos-
sibility. An approximate solution is still satisfactory provided that it is stable.
As systems can be continuous-time or discrete-time, algorithms should ideally
be able to deal with any possible setting.

                                        vii
viii                                                                     Preface


    Many references will be used to build our theory and it is already worth
underlining the thesis of Tom d’Haene [33] whose work on a related topic em-
phasized the control point of view whereas our contribution is best appreciated
from an optimization point of view. We focus on the development of innovative
formulations and efficient methods dedicated to the problem. We thus develop
several directions of research which potentially produce as many algorithms.
The first direction of research consists in developing an iterative algorithm
which works on the most usual formulation of the problem. We thus work in-
side a nonconvex feasible domain. The resulting algorithm is conceptually and
surprisingly simple given the complicated setting it must deal with.
    The second direction we develop focuses on algorithms which avoid the
complexity encountered in the first case by reformulating the problem. The
purpose of the reformulations is to provide an easier framework in which the
problem can be solved even though we will see they can appear more complex
at first.
    The third and final direction of research exploits the structure brought into
the problem by polynomials. We thus adapt our algorithms when possible and
investigate other ways of solving the polynomial problem.
    The main contributions of this thesis are given by the algorithms that we
detail throughout this thesis. Those algorithms are able to solve the nearest
stable system problem in several configurations : matrices and polynomials,
continuous-time and discrete-time, real and complex. Several possible alterna-
tive formulations are also suggested which could be used to solve the problem
as well. Another contribution is given by the survey from the literature related
to the nearest stable system and its particularities and the geometry of the
stable set.
    The results produced by our research were communicated in two publica-
tions in peer-reviewed journals [77, 76].
    Our manuscript is divided in four chapters.
                Chapter 1 recalls several theoretic concepts that are used in
                  this thesis. The content is intentionally limited to the most
                  important definitions and theorems which are used.
                Chapter 2 introduces the nearest stable system problem, ex-
                  plores the geometry of the stable set and describes optimal-
                  ity conditions for the problem. The chapter is essentially a
                  survey of the literature.
                Chapter 3 presents the results we obtained for matrices. Two
                  methods for solving the nearest stable matrix problems
                  are investigated in the chapter and convergence results are
                  given for both of them. The chapter also contains several
                  reformulations of the nearest stable system problem for the
                  continuous-time case.
                Chapter 4 is dedicated to polynomials. Some of the algo-
                  rithms contained in the previous chapter are extended to
                  handle polynomials. We also presents other algorithms
                                                     ix


which exploit the structure of the polynomials. The em-
phasis is put on the efficiency of the methods and some
time is thus taken to discuss related aspects.
Chapter 1

Preliminaries

In this chapter we give a general introduction to the background areas of our
research. The nearest stable system is at the crossroad of three main fields :
control, optimization and numerical linear algebra.
    Control is the essential field of our problem and it also provides the original
motivation for our problem. With its well-established theory, the optimization
field provides us with the tools to solve the problem in an efficient way. Because
of our focus on analytical solutions, numerical linear algebra is at the heart of
our work, and its use in our developments is widespread.
    This chapter is organized as follows :

                Section 1.1 recalls the most basic concepts of linear algebra
                   and also provides a more selective introduction to the math-
                   ematical objects we will use throughout : matrices and
                   polynomials.
                Section 1.2 introduces important notions of analysis such as
                   convexity of a set, normal and tangent cone to a set, differ-
                   entiability and illustrates them through several examples
                   that will be reused at multiple times.
                Section 1.3 emphasizes several results related to optimality
                   conditions, both necessary and sufficient. We choose to
                   present some results under the form of variational inequal-
                   ities which will be helpful to present necessary optimality
                   conditions for the nearest stable system in the second chap-
                   ter.
                Section 1.4 first presents several basic elements of systems
                   theory. Some time is then spent to present the spectral ab-
                   scissa and the spectral radius which are going to be used
                   occasionally in replacement of the Lyapunov stability cri-
                   terion.




                                        1
2                                                                       Chapter 1. Preliminaries


1.1         Linear Algebra
1.1.1       Norms and scalar products
A vector space is a set endowed with a commutative addition law and an
external composition law with respect to a a scalar field (F, +, ·). In our work,
F is most often the field of complex numbers C or the field of real numbers R.
Definition 1.1. Let E be such a vector space on a field F. Then a norm on
E is a function
                             k·k : E →R
such that ∀x ∈ E,
                             1) kxk ≥ 0
                             2) kxk = 0            ⇔       x=0
                             3)kαxk = |α|kxk              ∀α ∈ F .
Definition 1.2. An inner product on E is a function
                                   h·, ·i : E × E → F
that satisfies the following properties
       1)hαx + βy, zi = αhx, zi + βhy, zi,               ∀x, y, z ∈ E    and    ∀α, β ∈ F
       2)       hx, xi ≥ 0    ∀x ∈ E           and     hx, xi = 0 ⇔ x = 0
       3)        hx, yi = hy, xi     ∀x, y ∈ E .
    In this thesis, we work nearly exclusively with real-valued scalar products
and the third condition in Definition (1.2) is thus reduced to hx, yi = hy, xi.
                                                                      1
    All scalar products induce a norm by the relation k · k = hx, xi 2 but not
all norms are induced by a scalar product. The standard real-valued scalar
product on Cn is defined as
                                 (          )
                                   X
                     hx, yi = Re     xi y¯i      ∀x, y ∈ Cn
                                           i

and induces the usual 2−norm k · k2 on Cn . We denote by h·, ·iC the standard
complex-valued scalar product on Cn by
                                X
                      hx, yiC =   xi y¯i   ∀x, y ∈ Cn .
                                       i

    For a given norm k · k, we define the dual norm as
                                   kyk∗ = max hx, yi .                                      (1.1)
                                               kxk≤1

A norm is self-dual if k · k = k · k∗ .
Example 1. The 2-norm is self-dual since
                                   kyk2 = max hx, yi .
                                               kxk2 ≤1
1.1 Linear Algebra                                                           3


   Induced norms satisfy a number of useful properties some of which will be
extensively used in this manuscript.

Theorem 1.3 (Cauchy-Schwarz). Let E be a vector space over a field F,
equipped with a scalar product h·, ·i. Then ∀x, y ∈ E

                               |hx, yi| ≤ kxk∗ kyk .

   The Cauchy-Schwarz theorem is used to derive other algebraic properties;
probably the most well-known is the triangle inequality which we recall now.

Property 1.4 (Triangle inequality). Let E be a vector space equipped with an
induced norm k · k. Then, ∀x, y ∈ E

                              kx + yk ≤ kxk + kyk .

   The reverse triangle inequality that we now introduce is a consequence of
the triangle inequality applied to kx + y − yk.

Property 1.5 (Reverse triangle inequality). Let E be a vector space equipped
with a induced norm k · k. Then, ∀x, y ∈ E

                              kx + yk ≥ kxk − kyk .


Adjoint of an operator

Definition 1.6 (Linear operator). Let E and F be two vector spaces over a
field F such as R or C. A linear operator L is a function

                                   L : E→F

that satisfies the following properties

             L(αx + βy) = αL(x) + βL(y)        ∀x, y ∈ E   α, β ∈ F .

   Suppose that we have a linear operator L : E → F , where the two vector
spaces E and F are each equipped with a scalar product h·, ·iE and h·, ·iF
respectively.

Definition 1.7 (Adjoint of a linear operator). The adjoint L∗ of L is a linear
operator from F → E, such that for any x ∈ E and any y ∈ F

                             hLx, yiF = hx, L∗ yiE .                      (1.2)

    Moreover if L = A, A ∈ Cn×n , then L∗ is the conjugate transpose A∗ of A
which is also denoted by the asterisk. Naturally, the expression of the adjoint
of an operator is dependent on the scalar product which is used.
4                                                         Chapter 1. Preliminaries


1.1.2    Matrix, eigenvalue and positive definiteness
Let x be a vector in a vector space E. Vectors are represented using the column
convention, i.e,                   
                                   v1
                                   .. 
                              v =  .  , vi ∈ F∀i
                                   vn
A vector x = 0 if and only if all its elements are 0. By ei we denote a vector of
zeros with a 1 at the ith position.
   Let X be a matrix in a vector space E of dimension n × m over a field F. A
matrix X is composed of elements Xij ∈ F placed in an array which we write

                                X = [Xij ]n,m
                                          i,j=1 .

By [X]ij = Xij we denote the element of the matrix at the intersection of the
ith row and the j th column. Given a matrix X ∈ Cn×m , the transpose of a
matrix is denoted by X T ∈ Cm×n and satisfies [X T ]ij = Xji . Its conjugate
matrix X ∗ is an element of Cm×n and satisfies [X ∗ ]ij = X̄ji .
     A squared matrix is said to be symmetric if X T = X, anti-symmetric if
X = −X, Hermitian if X = X ∗ and skew-Hermitian (or anti-Hermitian) if
   T

X ∗ = −X.
     The trace operator of X ∈ Cn×n , denoted by Tr(·), returns the sum of its
diagonal elements. The determinant of a matrix is denoted by det(·).

Scalar product for matrices
The standard real-valued scalar product on Cn×n uses the trace operator Tr(·)
                                                           
                                              X            
                hX, Y i = Re {Tr(XY ∗ )} = Re      Xij Ȳij             (1.3)
                                                           
                                                    i,j

                                          qP
                                                         2
and induces the Frobenius norm kXkF =          i,j |Xij | . We will frequently use
the following properties associated to the Frobenius norm.

Property 1.8. Let X, Y, Z ∈ Cn×n and let h·, ·i be the scalar product associated
with the Frobenius norm. Then

                       hXY, Zi = hX, ZY ∗ i = hY, X ∗ Zi

   Given the importance of this property in this thesis, we prove the above
result.

Proof. We first prove that hXY, Zi = hZ, XY i. Indeed, since the real part of
the trace does not change under conjugation, we have

        hXY, Zi = Re {Tr(XY Z ∗ )} = Re {Tr((XY Z ∗ )∗ )} = hZ, XY i .
1.1 Linear Algebra                                                             5


Then, we can prove the first equality hXY, Zi = hX, ZY ∗ i by using associativity
of the matrix product,

        hXY, Zi = Re {Tr(XY Z ∗ )} = Re {Tr(X(ZY ∗ )∗ )} = hX, ZY ∗ i .

The second equality hXY, Zi = hY, X ∗ Zi is proved by using the identity
Tr(AB ∗ ) = Tr(B ∗ A) ∀A, B ∈ Cm×n . This identity implies that

                            hXY, Zi = Re {Tr(XY Z ∗ )}
                                    = Re {Tr(Z ∗ XY )}
                                    = hZ ∗ X, Y ∗ i
                                    = hY ∗ , Z ∗ Xi
                                    = hY, ZX ∗ i .



    The identity matrix of size n × n is denoted by In . When its dimensions
are clear from the context the subscript is omitted and we simply write I.
    A matrix U ∈ Cn×n is said to be unitary if U U ∗ = I = U ∗ U . The real
equivalent of a unitary matrix is called an orthogonal matrix V ∈ Rn×n and
satisfies V V T = I = V T V .

Example 2. A norm is said to be unitarily invariant if kU AV ∗ k = kAk for all
unitary matrices U and V . The Frobenius norm and the 2−norms are unitarily
invariant.

Matrix theory
We define two additional operator products in addition to the usual matrix
products.

Definition 1.9 (Hadamard product). Let X, Y ∈ Cn×n . Then the Hadamard
product is the element-wise product defined by

                               [X   Y ]ij = Xij Yij .

Definition 1.10 (Kronecker product). For any two matrices X ∈ Cna ×nb and
Y ∈ Cnc ×nd , the Kronecker product of X and Y is given by
                                                      
                                    X11 Y · · · X1n Y
                     Z = X ⊗ Y =  ...      ..     .. 
                                  
                                               .    . 
                                      Xn1 Y     ···     Xnn Y

where Z ∈ Cna nc ×nb nd .

    Note that unlike the Hadamard product, the Kronecker product is not com-
mutative. The Kronecker product is often used to obtain the matrix represen-
tation of a linear operator.
6                                                         Chapter 1. Preliminaries


Definition 1.11. Let X ∈ Fm×n . Then the operator vec(X) returns the vector
obtained by stacking up the columns of X, i.e, if X = [x1 · · · xn ] where xi ∈ Fn
is the ith column of X, then
                                         
                                         x1
                                         .. 
                               vec(X) =  .  .
                                             xn

Example 3. The following identity is well-known. For any three given complex
matrices X, Y and Z such that the product XY Z makes sense, then

                        vec(XY Z) = (Z T ⊗ X) vec(Y ) .

  Let us now introduce a class of matrices that will be frequently used in this
manuscript.
Definition 1.12 (Positive definite). A Hermitian matrix X ∈ Cn×n is called
positive definite, denoted X  0, if

                          v ∗ Xv > 0     ∀v ∈ Cn \{0} ,

and is called negative definite if −X  0.
Definition 1.13 (Positive semidefinite). A Hermitian matrix X ∈ Cn×n is
called positive semidefinite, denoted X  0, if

                            v ∗ Xv ≥ 0       ∀v ∈ Cn ,

and is called negative semidefinite if −X  0.
    We denote the set of all positive definite matrices of size n by Kn++ and the
set of all semidefinite positive matrices of size n by Kn+ .
    The following definition will be very useful.
Definition 1.14 (Cholesky factor). A matrix L ∈ Cn×n is a Cholesky factor
of X ∈ Cn×n if it is lower triangular and

                                   X = LL∗ .

Property 1.15 (Cholesky decomposition). The Cholesky decomposition of a
matrix X ∈ Kn++
                             X = LL∗
where L has a positive diagonal is unique.
    Let us now recall a number of properties related to eigenvalues.
Definition 1.16 (Eigenvalue). Let X ∈ Cn×m and let (λi , v) ∈ C × Cm be
such that
                          Xv = λi v, v 6= 0 .                      (1.4)
Then (λi , v) is called an eigenpair, λi is an eigenvalue of X and v is a right-
eigenvector associated with λi .
1.1 Linear Algebra                                                              7


    We sometimes denote the eigenvalue λi as λi (X) to prevent confusion. A
matrix X living in a space of dimension n has n, possibly non-distinct, eigen-
values. The set formed of all, possibly non-distinct, eigenvalues of X is called
the spectrum of X.
    A positive definite matrix X ∈ Kn++ has n positive eigenvalues.
    Let {λ1 , . . . , λn } be the spectrum of a matrix X ∈ Cn×n . A matrix X is
called singular if λi (X) = 0 for some i ∈ {1, . . . , n}.
Property 1.17 (Trace and determinant of a matrix). For any square matrix
X ∈ E, two eigenvalue functions of X are given by the trace and the determi-
nant of X and satisfy                X
                            Tr(X) =     λi (X) ,
                                          i
                                         Y
                              det(X) =        λi (X) .
                                         i

Definition 1.18 (Nonnegative matrix [50]). A matrix X ∈ Rn×n is said to be
nonnegative, denoted X ≥ 0, if
                         Xij ≥ 0      ∀i, j = 1, . . . , n .
Definition 1.19 (Irreducibility [50]). A nonnegative matrix X ∈ Rn×n is said
to be irreducible if there exists no permutation matrix P such that
                                                  
                                         X11 X12
                            P T XP =                 .
                                          0    X22
   The following well-known theorem is due to Perron and Frobenius.
Theorem 1.20 (Perron-Frobenius [50]). Suppose that a matrix X ∈ Rn×n is
nonnegative and irreducible. Then
  1. λmax ∈ R+ ;
  2. λmax is a simple eigenvalue of X;
  3. ∃u ∈ Rn , u > 0 : uT X = λmax uT .
   Even though we denote them differently, nonnegative matrices should not
be confounded with positive definite and positive semidefinite matrices.
   We now define the algebraic and geometric multiplicity of an eigenvalue.
Those definitions will be used for discussions related to the Jordan form of a
matrix and the singularities of the stable set.
Definition 1.21 (Algebraic multiplicity). Let λi be an eigenvalue of X ∈
Cn×n . Then we define the algebraic multiplicity ma (λi ) as the cardinality of λi
in the spectrum of X.
Definition 1.22 (Geometric multiplicity). Let λi be an eigenvalue of X ∈
Cn×n . The geometric multiplicity mg (λi ) is the dimension of the eigenspace
related to λi , i.e.
                      mg (λi ) = dim(Ker(λi I − X)),
where the operator Ker denotes the kernel (or nullspace) of a matrix.
8                                                                          Chapter 1. Preliminaries


Property 1.23. Let λi be an eigenvalue of X ∈ Cn×n . Then

                              1 ≤ mg (λi ) ≤ ma (λi ) .

In particular, if X has n distinct eigenvalues, then X has n distinct eigenvectors
and ma (λi ) = mg (λi ) = 1 .
    Algebraic and geometric multiplicities are useful to characterize the eigen-
structure of a matrix, i.e. the number of distinct eigenvalues and dimension of
the eigenspaces associated with them. The same information can be deduced
from some canonical matrix forms.
Theorem 1.24 (Jordan form). For any matrix X ∈ Cn×n , there exists a
nonsingular matrix T and a matrix XJ called the Jordan form of X, such that
T −1 XT = XJ which has the block diagonal structure
                                               
                                 B11
                          XJ = 
                                      ..       
                                          .     
                                                            Bjj

where Bii is a block diagonal matrix, i.e.,

                             Bii = diag(Jn(i)
                                           1
                                              , . . . , Jn(i)
                                                           s
                                                              )
                                                                      i


with only one (repeated) eigenvalue λi and
                                                                            
                                          λi          1                       
                                                                              
                                                    ..          ..          
                                                                              
                                                        .             .      
                  Jn(i)

The block Jnk is called a Jordan block associated with λi .
    The Jordan form of a matrix completely reveals the eigenstructure of a
matrix X. Indeed, as each diagonal block Bii contains only Jordan blocks as-
sociated with λi , the dimension of each block Bii gives the algebraic multiplicity
of λi , i.e,                               X
                                ma (λi ) =    nj .
                                                 j

Since the kernel of each Jordan block has dimension 1, the number of Jordan
blocks associated with λi gives the geometric multiplicity of λi , i.e.

                                     mg (λi ) = si .

Definition 1.25. An eigenvalue λi is called simple if ma (λi ) = mg (λi ) = 1,
or equivalently, if there is only one Jordan block associated with it and its
dimension is 1.
1.1 Linear Algebra                                                                9


Definition 1.26. An eigenvalue is called semisimple if mg (λi ) = ma (λi ), or
equivalently, if the size of the largest Jordan block associated to it is 1.

Definition 1.27. An eigenvalue λi is said to be nonderogatory if and only if
there is only one Jordan block J (i) associated with it, i.e. mg (λi ) = 1. The size
of this block then equals the algebraic multiplicity of the eigenvalue.

Definition 1.28 (Similarity [50]). A matrix B ∈ Cn×n is said to be similar to
a matrix X ∈ Cn×n if there exists a nonsingular matrix T ∈ Cn×n such that

                                  B = T −1 XT .

Definition 1.29. The subset of Cn×n which contains all the matrices similar
to X is called the (similarity) orbit of X and is written orb(X). Equivalently,
we can write

             orb(X) = {T −1 XT : T ∈ Cn×n , T is nonsingular} .


1.1.3     Polynomials
A polynomial p(λ) of degree n on a field F is a function

           p(λ) : C → C : p(λ) = pn λn + · · · + p1 λ + p0 ,     pn 6= 0      (1.5)
                                                                        
whose coefficients pi ∈ F, i = 1, . . . n. The vector pT = pn · · · p0 ∈ Fn+1
is called the vector of coefficients. The polynomial p(λ) is said to be a complex
polynomial when F = C and to be a real polynomial when F = R. A polynomial
is said to be monic if pn = 1.
    An alternative formulation to (1.5) is obtained through the use of the stan-
dard complex-valued scalar product :

                                 p(λ) = hp, πλn iC

where πλn is the vector
                                         n
                                         λ
                                         .. 
                                  πλn =  .  .
                                         
                                        λ
                                          1

We say that ri ∈ C is a root of p(λ) if p(ri ) = 0.

Theorem 1.30 (Fundamental theorem of algebra). A polynomial of degree n
has n, possibly non-distinct, roots.

   The roots of a real polynomial are either real or occur in complex conjugate
pairs. By p̄(λ) we denote the polynomial obtained from the conjugate p̄ of p

                                 p̄(λ) = hp̄, πλn i .

                                    p(r) = [p(λ; r)]c

the vector of coefficients p ∈ Cn+1 of the polynomial p(λ; r).
   Polynomials and matrices are linked through the characteristic polynomial.
Let X ∈ Cn×n . Then the characteristic polynomial x(λ) is obtained as

                                   x(λ) = det(λI − X)

and the eigenvalues of X are the roots of the characteristic polynomial x(λ).

1.2      Analysis
1.2.1     Sets
In the following we consider a vector space E equipped with the standard inner
product h·, ·i on E and the associated induced norm k · k.
    We note by C ⊂ E the inclusion of C in E. The union of two sets C1 and C2
is C1 ∪ C2 , their intersection is written C1 ∩ C2 and the difference of two sets is
denoted C1 \C2 .
    Let a set C ⊂ E. We denote the interior of C by int C. The closure of C is
denoted by cl(C). The boundary of C are the elements obtained as

                                   cl(C)\ int C .

A set is said to be closed if it contains all its limit points. It is bounded if it
contains no half line. A set which is both closed and bounded is called compact.
Definition 1.31 (Convex set). Consider a set C ⊂ E. We say that C is convex
if and only if for any x, y ∈ C

                         θx + (1 − θ)y ∈ C        ∀θ ∈ [0, 1] .

   A set which is not convex will be called nonconvex.
   We also introduce the general definition of cone and present the cones that
we will use at some point in this manuscript.
12                                                                  Chapter 1. Preliminaries




                            TC (x̂)
                                                          TC (x̂)



                                      →
                                      −
                                      n
                                                                               NC (x̂)

                             NC (x̂) = {−
                                        →
                                        n}


Figure 1.2: Representation of the tangent and the normal cones on two different
sets.



Definition 1.32 (Cone). A set K ⊂ E is a cone if and only if 0 ∈ K and
∀x ∈ K
                          tx ∈ K, ∀t > 0 .

      An example of a cone is given by the set Kn+ of positive semidefinite matrices.

Definition 1.33 (Convex cone). A cone K is said to be convex if K is nonempty
and
                 Xp
                    λi xi ∈ K, ∀xi ∈ K and λi ≥ 0, p ∈ N .
                      i=1

Definition 1.34 (Dual cone). For any cone K ⊂ E the dual, or polar, of K
noted K ∗ is given by

                             K ∗ = {y | hy, xi ≤ 0, ∀x ∈ K} .

   The dual of a cone is always closed and therefore the dual of the dual,
noted (K ∗ )∗ is cl(K). We now give three examples that will be useful to our
developments.

Example 4 (Tangent and normal cone to a set [86]). Let x̂ ∈ cl(C) ⊂ E.
Then the normal and tangent cones1 to C at x̂ denoted by NC (x̂) and TC (x̂)
respectively are given by

                NC (x̂) = {y ∈ E |hy, x − x̂i ≤ o(kx − x̂k),         ∀x ∈ C} ,
                TC (x̂) = NC∗ (x̂)
     1 The definition of normal and tangent cones given here holds only under the assumption

that the set C is regular in the sense of Clarke at x̂. However, in this manuscript we will not
deal with the nonregular case. The definition of Clarke regularity can be found in Definition
6.4 in [86]
1.2 Analysis                                                                  13


where the term o(t) denotes a term which tends to zero at least linearly as
t → 0.
   The tangent and the normal cones are closed and convex. Though the for-
mulas make sense for any point in C, they both reduce to {0} when x̂ ∈ int C.
They can be easily represented as is shown in Figure 1.2.
Example 5 (Positive hull [86]). Any set can be lifted into a cone. We give
one way of performing this. Indeed, consider a set C ⊂ E, then the set
                       pos C = {tx | x ∈ C, t ≥ 0} ∪ {0}
is called the positive hull of C and is clearly a cone on E × R.

1.2.2    Functions
We now explore a number of concepts related to functional analysis. We sup-
pose throughout that the functions we are working with are lower-semicontinuous
and are Clarke regular in the sense of [86]. These assumptions simplify our de-
velopments and avoid the necessity to address a number of cases which will not
be encountered in this manuscript.
    For a function f : E → R ∪ {+∞} the domain of f , denoted dom f is the
set
                       dom f = {x ∈ E | |f (x)| < ∞} .
In order to prove the existence of the solutions to minimization problems, we
will frequently use the notion of level sets of a function which we introduce
next.
Definition 1.35 (Level sets). Let f be a real-valued function. The level sets
of f is
               LC0 = {x ∈ dom f | f (x) ≤ C0 , C0 fixed} .
   A function f on a set C with closed bounded level sets is said to be closed
on C.

Differentiability
We will frequently talk about smooth functions. The notion of smoothness is
intrinsically linked to the one of differentiability and directional derivatives.
Let E and F be two vector spaces.
Definition 1.36 (Directional derivative). Given a function f : E → F , the
directional derivative Df (x)[h] of f at x in the direction h ∈ E is given by
                                        f (x + th) − f (x)
                     Df (x)[h] = lim+                      .                (1.9)
                                  t→0            t
   A function f : E → F is differentiable at x ∈ E if there exists an
approximation of the function such that
                     f (x + h) = f (x) + Df (x)[h] + o(khk)               (1.10)
where the notation o(t) denotes terms that are decreasing at least linearly. This
can be defined more precisely using the notion of limits.
14                                                             Chapter 1. Preliminaries


Definition 1.37 (Differentiability). A function f : E → F is said to be
differentiable at x ∈ dom f if and only if ∃Df (x)[h] ∈ F
                           kf (x + h) − f (x) − Df (x)[h]k
                    lim                                    =0.
                   khk→0                 khk
    A function f is differentiable if it is differentiable everywhere on dom f . A
function f is said to be of class C (k) if it is k times continuously differentiable
everywhere on dom f and the kth derivative is continuous on dom f . A function
f is said to be smooth if f is of class C (2) at least. When f is a differentiable
real-valued scalar function, Definition 1.37 implies that Df (x)[h] is linear in h
and is given by
                             Df (x)[h] = h∇f (x), hi ,
where ∇f denotes the gradient of f .
    Instead of using Definition 1.36, one can also use the relation (1.10) and
deduce the expression of the gradient from the first order approximation of
the function; this is however equivalent to the use of the Definition 1.36 of
directional derivative. Directional derivatives of higher order can be obtained
by applying recursively the definition (1.9). For example, we have
                                          Df (x + th)[h] − Df (x)[h]
                D2 f (x)[h, h] = lim+
                                   t→0                t
Given a real-valued scalar function f of class C (3) , we have the following iden-
tities
                     Df (x)[h]       = h∇f (x), hi
                       D2 f (x)[h, h]     = h∇2 f (x)[h], hi
                       D3 f (x)[h, h, h] = hD3 f (x)[h, h], hi .
Directional derivatives satisfy the symmetry property, i.e.
               D2 f (x)[h1 , h2 ] = D2 f (x)[h2 , h1 ]   ∀h1 , h2 ∈ E .
   Let us illustrate the use of directional derivatives in the computation of the
gradient of a function.
Example 6. Let f : Cn×n → Cn×n be given by
                                    f (X) = X −1 .
If we use the definition given by equation (1.9), we can compute the directional
derivative of f in a given direction H ∈ Cn×n
                   f (X + tH) − f (X)        (X + tH)−1 − X −1
Df (X)[H] = lim                       = lim
              t→0+          t           t→0+          t
                                             (X + tH)−1 (I − (X + tH)X −1 )
                                      = lim+
                                        t→0                 t
                                             (X + tH) (X − (X + tH))X −1
                                                      −1
                                      = lim+
                                        t→0                  t
                                      = −X −1 HX −1 .
1.2 Analysis                                                                        15


Example 7. Let us now compute the directional derivative of the log det func-
tion f (X) : Kn+ → R : X → − log det(X). Let H ∈ Kn+ and let us compute
the first order approximation of the function from which we will deduce the
gradient of the function
                                             1           1       1       1
        − log det(X + tH) = − log det(X 2 (I + tX − 2 HX − 2 )X 2 )
                                                                     1       1
                           = − log det(X) − log det(I + tX − 2 HX − 2 )
                                                                 1      1
                                            X
                           = − log det(X) −     log(1 + tλi (X − 2 HX − 2 ))
                                                 i

The first order approximation of log(1 + tλi ) around t = 0 gives log(1 + tλi ) ≈
tλi . Therefore,
                                                            1      1
                                                 X
          − log det(X + tH) = − log det(X) − t      λi (X − 2 HX − 2 ) .
                                                     i

Following the application of the limit (1.9), we get
                                                  1      1
                                       X
                      Df (X)[H] = −       λi (X − 2 HX − 2 )
                                         i
                                                 1           1
                                   = − Tr(X − 2 HX − 2 )
                                   = h−X −1 , Hi
where the last equality is deduced from the properties of the scalar product given
in Property 1.8.
    In many cases, the computation of the derivatives can be simplified by using
the chain rule of the function. The frequent use of the chain rule that we make
in this manuscript encourages us to develop and illustrate the concept here.
    Let us consider three nonempty sets X , Y and Z ∈ E. We define the
composition function
                       F : X → Z : F (x) = (f ◦ g)(x) ,
where
                                   g : X →Y
                                   f : Y→Z
are differentiable on their domain. Then the chain rule states that
                        DF (x)[h] = Df (g(x))[Dg(x)[h]] .                        (1.11)
Let us see two examples of its application.
Example 8. Let us compute the directional derivative of the function
                            F (X) = − log det(A(X)) ,
where A(X) is a quadratic operator in X. Thus,
                               g(X) = A(X)
                               f (Y ) = − log det(Y )
16                                                         Chapter 1. Preliminaries


We have seen in example 7 that ∇f (Y ) = −Y −1 . Therefore

                       DF (X)[H] = h∇f, Dg(X)[H]i
                                    = h−Y −1 , DA(X)[H]i
                                    = h−D∗ A(X)[Y −1 ], Hi .

The first order directional derivative being always linear in H, its adjoint is
easily obtained.
    The chain rule can also be applied for higher order derivatives. Indeed, we
can compute the directional derivative of the chain rule following the usual rule
of derivation

D (Df (x)[Dg(x)[h]]) [h] = D2 f (x)[Dg(x)[h], Dg(x)[h]] + Df (x)[D2 g(x)[h, h]] .

A good example is obtained if we continue the preceding example.
Example 9. Let F (X) be given by

                             F (X) = − log det(A(X)) ,

as before. We have seen that the first order derivative of X −1 was given by

                           D(−X −1 )[H] = X −1 HX −1 .

Therefore, the second order derivative of F (X) is thus

D2 F (X)[H, H] = hX −1 DA(X)[H]X −1 , DA(X)[H]i+h−X −1 , D2 A(X)[H, H]i

where D2 A(X)[H, H] is now a quadratic function of H.
   When a function is nonsmooth at a point x̂, the gradient ∇f at x̂ cannot
be computed. Still an alternative can be used to replace the gradient.
Definition 1.38 (Subdifferential [86]). Let f : E → R ∪ {+∞}, the subdiffer-
ential of f at x̂ ∈ cl(dom f ) is the set

     ∂f = {y ∈ E |f (x) ≥ f (x̂) + hy, x − x̂i + o(kx − x̂k), ∀x ∈ dom f } .

If f is infinite at x̂, then ∂f (x̂) = ∅.
    Even when the function is differentiable, the few rules we provided until
now do not always suffice to obtain an accurate expression of the gradient. As
an example consider that x is a point on a manifold M. Then by definition,
the gradient ∇f (x) of the function f : M → R must belong to the tangent
plane of M at x. Whenever the computed gradient does not belong to the
tangent plane, it can be projected onto it to obtain the correct expression. We
illustrate the underlying principles in an illustrative example obtained for the
manifold of orthogonal matrices. The theory related to it is too long to be
included in this manuscript and we therefore refer to [1] for the theory along
with the proofs and developments associated with the example.
1.2 Analysis                                                                    17


Example 10 (Tangent plane to the manifold of orthogonal matrices). Let the
manifold M ⊂ Cn×n be defined by

                            M = {U ∈ Cn×n | U ∗ U = I}

A simple but not rigorous derivation of the tangent plane TM to M consists in
computing the directional derivative of U ∗ U = I in a direction S to obtain

                       TM = {S ∈ Cn×n | S ∗ U + U S ∗ = 0} .                 (1.12)

Now let us suppose that we have a real-valued differentiable function whose
domain is the manifold M, i.e

                             f : M → R : U → f (U ) .

The directional derivative of f at Û along a direction H ∈ Cn×n is given
by Df (Û ) = h∇f (Û ), Hi where ∇f (Û ) belongs to TM . Suppose now that the
computation yields a computed gradient, noted ∇fˆ(Û ), which does not belong to
the tangent plane. Then, ∇fˆ(Û ) can be projected onto TM using the orthogonal
projector PTM defined by
                                          1
                    PTM (∇fˆ(Û )) = ∇fˆ − Û (Û ∗ ∇fˆ + ∇fˆ∗ Û ) .        (1.13)
                                          2
One can thus verify easily by injecting (1.13) into (1.12) that

                                PTM (∇fˆ(Û )) ∈ TM .

By definition, for any direction H ∈ TM we have

                  Df (Û )[H] = h∇fˆ(Û ), Hi = hPTM (∇fˆ(Û )), Hi .

Indeed, the component of ∇fˆ(Û ) orthogonal to TM is orthogonal to H as well.
   In the same way, the theory in [1] can be used to show that ∇f (X) is
symmetric if X is symmetric and diagonal if X is diagonal.

Convexity
The notion of convexity which we briefly recalled in the previous section applies
to functions as well.
Definition 1.39 (Convex function). A function f : E → R ∪ {+∞} is convex
if and only if dom f is convex and for any x, y ∈ dom f ,

               f (θx + (1 − θ)y) ≤ θf (x) + (1 − θ)f (y),    ∀θ ∈ [0, 1] .   (1.14)

   By definition, a convex function of class C (2) satisfies both ∇2 f (x)  0 and
the inequality

                  f (y) ≥ f (x) + h∇f (x), y − xi    ∀x, y ∈ dom f .         (1.15)

If −f is convex, f is said to be concave.
18                                                            Chapter 1. Preliminaries


Property 1.40 (Positive sum of convex functions [16]). Let f1 and f2 be
two convex functions on dom f1 and dom f2 respectively. Then for any two
w1 , w2 ≥ 0
                            f = w1 f1 + w2 f2
is convex on dom f1 ∩ dom f2 .

Property 1.41 (Pointwise maximum of convex functions [16]). Let f1 (x) and
f2 (x) be two convex functions on dom f1 and dom f2 respectively. Then the
pointwise maximum of f1 and f2 defined as

                            f (x) = max f1 (x), f2 (x)

is convex on dom f = dom f1 ∩ dom f2 .

Property 1.42 (Affine invariance [16]). Let f : E → R be a convex function
and let A(x) + b : F → E be an affine operator then

                                    f (A(x) + b)

is convex.

Lipschitz continuity
The concept of Lipschitz continuity is very useful to estimate the local change
of magnitude of a function f . It is used to bound these variations. In that
prospect and in this subsection, k · k denotes any norm induced by a scalar
product.

Definition 1.43 (Lipschitz continuity [86]). A differentiable function f (x) :
E → R has a Lipschitz continuous gradient on a convex set C if there exists a
positive constant L, called the Lipschitz constant, such that for any two points
x and x̂ ∈ C
                      k∇f (x) − ∇f (x̂)k∗ ≤ Lkx − x̂k ,                   (1.16)

    A sufficient condition for a Lipschitz continuous gradient is given by the
following condition

Property 1.44 ([73, 86]). A function f of class C (2) has a continuous Lipschitz
gradient with constant L on C if and only if

                            max k∇2 f (x)[h]k∗ ≤ L .
                            khk=1

   As a consequence of this last property, functions with Lipschitz continuous
gradient can be bounded from above as the next property explains.

Property 1.45 ([86]). If a function f of class C (1) has a Lipschitz continuous
gradient on the convex set C with constant L, then for any x and x̂ ∈ C,
                                                        L
                 f (x) ≤ f (x̂) + h∇f (x̂), x − x̂i +     kx − x̂k2 .
                                                        2
1.2 Analysis                                                                   19


Self-concordant functions
Definition 1.46 (Self-concordant function [73]). A closed convex function
F (y) of class C (3) with open domain is a self-concordant function if
                                                         3
               |D3 F (y)[h, h, h]| ≤ MF (D2 F (y)[h, h]) 2    ∀h ∈ E       (1.17)

holds for any y ∈ dom F and some constant MF ≥ 0.
   If the constant MF = 2 the function is called a standard self-concordant
function.
Example 11 (Quadratic function). Any quadratic function is self-concordant.
Indeed, let F = hQx, xi + hc, xi + d, then

                D2 F (x)[h, h] = h2Qh, hi       D3 F (x)[h, h, h] = 0

Therefore, it is self-concordant with constant MF = 0.
Example 12 (log function). The function F : R → R ∪ {+∞}
                            
                              − log(x) if x ≥ 0
                    F (x) =
                              +∞        otherwise

is a standard self-concordant function. Indeed we have
                                      1               −2
                             F 00 =         F 000 =      ,
                                      x2              x3
which satisfy the inequality (1.17).
   Self-concordant functions have interesting properties, notably of being affine-
invariant and of being a barrier function on the closure of their domain.
Property 1.47 (Affine-invariant property [73]). Let A(x) + b be an affine
operator and assume that a function F (y) is self-concordant with the constant
MF . Then the function φ(x) = F (A(x) + b) is also self-concordant and Mφ =
MF .
Property 1.48 (Positive sum [73]). Let F1 and F2 be two self-concordant
functions with constants M1 and M2 and let w1 , w2 > 0. Then the function

                                 F = w1 F1 + w2 F2

is a self-concordant function for dom F = dom F1 ∩ dom F2 with constant
                                    1      1
                         MF = max( √ M1 , √ M2 ).
                                    w1     w2

   Two fundamental results associated with self-concordant functions are given
by the following theorems.
Theorem 1.49 ([73]). Let the function F be self-concordant. If dom F contains
no straight line, then the Hessian F 00 of F is nonsingular at any x ∈ dom F .
20                                                               Chapter 1. Preliminaries


Theorem 1.50 (Barrier function [73]). Let F be a self-concordant function.
Then for any point x̂ belonging to the boundary of dom F and any sequence
                            {xk } ⊂ dom F : xk → x̂
we have F (xk ) → +∞.
Definition 1.51 (Self-concordant barrier [73] ). A standard self-concordant
function F (x) is a ν-self-concordant barrier for the set dom F ⊂ E, if
                     max[2hF 0 (x), ui − hF 00 (x)[u], ui] ≤ ν .                  (1.18)
                     u∈E

In particular if F 00 (x) is nonsingular, (1.18) amounts to
                         h(F 00 (x))−1 F 0 (x), F 0 (x)i ≤ ν .
    The definition of self-concordant barrier is only needed to introduce the
following definition which will be central in our developments.
Definition 1.52 (Analytic center [73]). Let F (x) be a ν-self-concordant barrier
for the set dom F . The point
                            x∗,F = arg min F (x)
                                          x∈dom F

is called the analytic center of the convex set dom F , generated by the barrier
F (x).
    Self-concordant functions are a good class of functions on which one can
apply the Newton method. Indeed, the Newton method is affine invariant and
therefore it does not depend on the metric which is used. Likewise, the metric
defined by the Hessian of any self-concordant function is also affine-invariant.
Therefore the convergence results obtained from an application of the Newton
method on a self-concordant function are very favorable as underlined in [73].


1.3     Optimality conditions
Optimization is a field of mathematics and engineering focused on the con-
struction of algorithms and/or mathematical conditions for characterizing the
solutions of a minimization problem. Because of its existent and future impli-
cations in many other fields and real-life applications, optimization is a very
active field.
    In the following, we understand by optimization problem any minimization
problem, and accordingly, we agree on the fact that an optimization problem
always is a minimization problem unless stated otherwise.
    The goal is to find the minimum of a real-valued function f (x) over some
feasible set C. As our focus will go to constrained problems we now present
optimality conditions for them only. In a first step, we can differentiate between
implicitly and explicitly constrained minimization problems. A minimization
problem is explicitly constrained if explicit functional constraints are used to
describe the feasible set. Whenever explicit functional constraints are not given,
the problem is implicitly constrained.
1.3 Optimality conditions                                                       21


1.3.1     Optimality conditions for implicitly constrained op-
          timization problems
In its most basic form, an unconstrained optimization problem is written
                                      inf f (x)
                                      x∈C

where we suppose that C ⊂ E is nonempty and f (x) is continuous on C. The
notation inf denotes the fact that the optimal solution might not be obtained,
hence the search for an infimum. If additionally we suppose that f (x) is closed
on C, i.e. its level sets are compact on C, then a minimum exists and we can
write
                                  min f (x) .                             (1.19)
                                  x∈C

A minimization problem is said to be convex if both the objective function and
the feasible set are convex. As we will see, convex optimization problems have
much favorable properties compared to nonconvex ones.
   A candidate solution x̂ is a global optimal solution if and only if

                             f (x) ≥ f (x̂)       ∀x ∈ C .

Checking global optimality is very hard in general and alternative optimality
conditions are sought. If we suppose that f is differentiable at x̂, we can locally
approximate f (x) by its Taylor expansion

                   f (x) = f (x̂) + h∇f (x̂), x − x̂i + o(kx − x̂k)

where we recall that the notation o(t) denotes terms that satisfy
                                            o(t)
                                      lim        =0.
                                   t→0       t
Therefore, x̂ is locally optimal if

                f (x) − f (x̂) = h∇f (x̂), x − x̂i + o(kx − x̂k) ≥ 0 .

We can rewrite this last condition as

                          h−∇f (x̂), x − x̂i ≤ o(kx − x̂k)

or equivalently, following our definition of the normal cone to a point (2.41)

                                −∇f (x̂) ∈ NC (x̂) .

This last result amounts to a necessary condition for local optimality and is
equivalent to the following condition related to the tangent cone.
Theorem 1.53 (First order necessary local optimality conditions [86, Theorem
6.12]). If a point x̂ ∈ C is a local optimal solution of the minimization problem
(1.19) with f being differentiable at x̂ then

                     h∇f (x̂), x − x̂i ≥ 0      ∀x ∈ x̂ + TC (x̂) .         (1.20)

In particular, if x̂ ∈ int C, (1.20) implies that ∇f (x̂) = 0.
22                                                                   Chapter 1. Preliminaries


   Any point which satisfies Theorem 1.53 is called a stationary point. If
additionally C is a convex set then (1.20) is equivalent to
                         h∇f (x̂), x − x̂i ≥ 0         ∀x ∈ C .
Let us now state a global result for convex optimization problems.
Theorem 1.54 (Necessary and sufficient first order optimality conditions [16]).
Let f ∈ C (1) be the objective function of a convex minimization problem. Then
x̂ ∈ C is a global optimal solution of the minimization problem if and only if
                         h∇f (x̂), x − x̂i ≥ 0         ∀x ∈ C .                       (1.21)
In particular, if x̂ ∈ int C, the condition (1.21) simplifies to
                                    ∇f (x̂) = 0 .

1.3.2     Optimality conditions for explicitly constrained op-
          timization problems
A constrained minimization problem with scalar constraints takes the form
                         min f0 (x)
                         x∈E
                          s.t   hi (x) = 0        i = 1, . . . , k                    (1.22)
                                fi (x) ≤ 0        i = 1, . . . , m
where we suppose that the constraints define a nonempty set in the vector
space E and f0 (x) is closed on the domain C defined by the intersection of
the equality constraints hi (x) = 0, i = 1, . . . , k and inequality constraints
fi (x) ≤ 0, i = 1, . . . , m.
     The problem (1.22) is called the primal problem in contrast to the dual
problem which we introduce now.
     In order to solve the primal problem (1.22) one can basically lift the con-
straints into the objective using a weighted sum of the constraints. We obtain
the function
                                         k
                                         X                   m
                                                             X
                 L(x, µ, λ) = f0 (x) +         µi hi (x) +         λi fi (x) ,        (1.23)
                                         i=1                 i=1

where µ and λ are called the vectors of Lagrange multipliers or dual variables.
We call L(x, µ, λ) the Lagrangian of the problem.
   If f0 is differentiable, the dual function is obtained by minimizing the La-
grangian (1.23) over x to get
                            g(µ, λ) = inf       L(x, µ, λ) .
                                         x∈C

It is well-known that g(µ, λ) is concave independently of whether f0 is convex
or not. Therefore, the dual problem defined as
                                    max g(µ, λ)
                                     µ,λ
                                                                                      (1.24)
                                    s.t.     λ≥0
1.4 Systems and Stability                                                         23


is a convex problem. The optimal value g∗ of (1.24) satisfies the weak duality
property
                                g∗ ≤ f0,∗ .                             (1.25)
Whenever (1.25) is active, i.e.
                                       g∗ = f0,∗
we say that strong duality holds.

Theorem 1.55 (Necessary local optimality conditions [16]). Let x∗ and (µ∗ , λ∗ )
be any two primal and dual points such that strong duality holds and the gradi-
ent of the active constraints are linearly independent, then it also satisfies the
Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions defined as

                      ∇L(x∗ , µ∗ , λ∗ ) = 0                                   (1.26)
                                hi (x∗ ) = 0       i = 1, . . . , k           (1.27)
                                fi (x∗ ) ≤ 0       i = 1, . . . , m           (1.28)
                                   λi,∗ ≥ 0        i = 1, . . . , m           (1.29)
                            λi,∗ fi (x∗ ) = 0      i = 1, . . . , m .         (1.30)

Moreover if the primal is convex, the KKT conditions are sufficient for the
existence of a local minimum at x∗ .

    The conditions (1.26)-(1.29) can easily be derived as the first order opti-
mality conditions that the primal and the dual must both satisfy. Equation
(1.30) is called the complementary slackness condition and implies that the
Lagrange multipliers associated with non-active inequality constraints are zero
at the optimum.
    Note that Theorem 1.55 states a necessary condition for local optimality on
the condition that strong duality holds but independently of whether the primal
is convex or not. Still, strong duality frequently does not hold for nonconvex
functions.

Theorem 1.56 (Necessary and sufficient conditions for global optimality [7]).
Let the primal (1.22) be convex and have a feasible set with nonempty interior.
Then x∗ is a global optimal solution of (1.22) if and only if there exists a dual
pair (µ∗ , λ∗ ) such that (x∗ , µ∗ , λ∗ ) satisfies the KKT conditions (1.26)-(1.30).


1.4      Systems and Stability
1.4.1     Systems
A system is generally written as a set of differential equations
                          
                             ẋ(t) = f (t, x(t), u(t))
                             y(t) = h(t, x(t), u(t)) ,

where t is the time, x(t) is the state of the system, ẋ is the derivative of x with
respect to the time, u(t) is called the input of the system and y(t) is called the
24                                                      Chapter 1. Preliminaries


output of the system. In this thesis our attention goes to Linear Time Invariant
(LTI) systems which have a state-space representation of the form
                               
                                 ẋ = Ax + Bu
                                                                          (1.31)
                                 y = Cx + Du ,

where the dependence on time of x, y and u is made implicit. In (1.31), A is the
state matrix. When the system is a single-input-single-output system, x ∈ Cn ,
y, u ∈ C, A ∈ Cn×n B, C T ∈ Cn and D is a scalar.
    By s we denote the continuous-time differentiation operator obtained by
the Laplace transform. By z we denote the discrete-time displacement oper-
ator obtained by the z-transform. When developments are common to the
continuous-time and discrete-time we prefer the use of the more general nota-
tion λ which thus denotes expressions that are applicable to both s and z.
    The transfer function of the system (1.31) is thus written

                        H(λ) = C(λI − A)−1 B + D .                        (1.32)

Transfer functions are rational functions of λ. The transfer function(1.32)
admits a representation as a fraction of two polynomials
                                        hb, πλn iC
                               H(λ) =                                     (1.33)
                                        ha, πλn iC
where ha, πλn iC = det(λI − A) and hb, πλn iC = (CΦB + D), where Φ/(det(λI −
A)) = (λI − A)−1 . It should be noted that a(λ) = ha, πλn iC is a monic polyno-
mial and thus an = 1.
   The roots of the numerator of (1.33) are called the zeros of the transfer
function. The roots of the denominator of (1.33) are called the poles of the
transfer function.
Remark 1.57. In order to avoid unnecessary repetitions in our manuscript,
we will use the system terminology for discussions common to polynomials and
matrices. Therefore, by “system” one should understand the state space matrix
A or its characteristic polynomial a(λ). By “poles” of the system one should
understand the corresponding eigenvalues of A or the roots of a(λ).
Definition 1.58 (Möbius transform). The Möbius transform is a continuous-
discrete transformation defined as
                                         1+s
                               s→z=          .
                                         1−s
Moreover, the inverse transformation is given by
                                         z+1
                               z→s=          .
                                         z−1
Property 1.59. The Möbius transform is a mapping that satisfies

                           |z| ≤ 1 for Re {s} ≤ 0 ,

and vice-versa. In particular the imaginary axis is mapped onto the unit circle.
1.4 Systems and Stability                                                        25


1.4.2     Stability
Definition 1.60 (Continuous-time stability). In continuous-time a system is
said to be (asymptotically) stable if and only if its poles are all located in the
open left half-plane in C.

Definition 1.61 (Discrete-time stability). In discrete-time, a system is said
to be stable if and only if all its poles are all located in the open unit disk of C
centered at the origin.

    These definitions are somehow easy to check because one only needs to
consider the poles of the transfer function but they imply that one is working
in the spectral space. Another way of evaluating the stability of a system, this
time in the coefficient space, was developed by Lyapunov.

Theorem 1.62 (Lyapunov). [65, 58] A matrix X ∈ Cn×n is continuously
(resp. discretely) stable if and only if there exists P ∈ Kn++ such that the
continuous-time map
                                def
                        AP (X) = ΨX (P ) = XP + P X ∗ ,                      (1.34)

or, respectively, the discrete-time map
                                def
                        AP (X) = ΨX (P ) = XP X ∗ − P                        (1.35)

is negative definite. Moreover, if X is stable and ΨX (P ) ≺ 0, then P  0.

    We call such P a Lyapunov (or stability) certificate for X. Such a certificate
is not unique, xo we can define the set PX of Lyapunov certificates of a matrix
X,
                      PX = {P ∈ Kn++ | − ΨX (P )  0} .
We can also give a definition for the set Sn of stable matrices in terms of
Lyapunov operators,

                  Sn = {X ∈ Cn×n |∃P ∈ Kn++ : −AP (X)  0} .

Let us now cite a corollary to the last theorem.

Corollary 1.63 ([58, Theorem 11 and 12]). For any continuous-time (resp.
discrete-time) X ∈ Sn and any Q ∈ Kn++ , there always exists a unique P ∈ Kn++
such that

                               XP + P X ∗ = −Q ,

or, respectively,

                               XP X ∗ − P = −Q ,

and vice-versa.
26                                                          Chapter 1. Preliminaries


Remark 1.64. Note that Theorem 1.62 makes use of the definition of negative
definite Hermitian matrices, which implies that AP (X) has to be Hermitian.
This is always guaranteed by the fact that P is Hermitian, and the whole ex-
pression makes sense.
Remark 1.65. The Lyapunov (1.34) and Stein (1.35) operators are linear in
P but the Stein operator is quadratic in X. Nonetheless, in order to ease the
notational burden, we will denote both operators by AP (X) when considering
X as the variable and will only distinguish the two when necessary.

1.4.3     Other measures of stability
The Lyapunov (1.34) and Stein (1.35) inequalities are not the only available
options to check the stability of a matrix. The spectral abscissa and the spec-
tral radius provide descriptions of the stability regions in continuous- and in
discrete-time respectively through simple constraints. Both are analytic spec-
tral functions that imply the knowledge of the eigenvalues of the matrix.
Definition 1.66. Given X ∈ Cn×n , the spectral abscissa is defined as
                                 def
                          α(X) = max Re {λi (X)} .                           (1.36)
                                           i

Definition 1.67. Given X ∈ Cn×n , the spectral radius is defined as
                                    def
                             ρ(X) = max |λi (X)| .                           (1.37)
                                               i

    The definitions (1.66) and (1.67) are easily adapted to polynomials. Indeed,
if one uses companion matrices X(x), x ∈ Cn , the definitions (1.66) and (1.67)
particularize to
                               def
                          α(x) = max Re {λi (X(x))} ,                      (1.38)
                                       i

and
                                 def
                            ρ(x) = max |λi (X(x))| ,                         (1.39)
                                           i

respectively, where λi (X(x)) now denotes the ith root of the characteristic
polynomial x(λ) = det(λI − X). Equations (1.38) and (1.39) are called the
root abscissa and root radius respectively.
     Our definition of spectral abscissa enable us to define the concept of active
set.
Definition 1.68. The active set is the set of indices M corresponding to active
eigenvalues, defined by M = {i : Re(λi (X)) = α(X)} in continuous-time, and
by M = {i : |λi (X)| = ρ(X)}.
  From our definitions, a continuous-time (resp. discrete-time) system X ∈
Cn×n will be stable if and only if

                         α(X) < 0          and ρ(X) < 1 ,

respectively.
1.4 Systems and Stability                                                       27


    It is well-known, [23, 21, 25, 24, 79, 97] that the spectral abscissa and the
spectral radius, and their polynomial counterpart, are nonsmooth and non-
differentiable functions of their arguments. Those functions indeed feature
singularities at the points corresponding to multiple eigenvalues.
    Whenever a single simple eigenvalue of X is active, the directional deriva-
tives of the spectral abscissa and the spectral radius are smooth functions of
their argument and, in that case, they are thus differentiable functions. When
two or more simple eigenvalues are active, the spectral abscissa and the spectral
radius are nonsmooth but they are nonetheless Lipschitz continuous.

Directional derivatives of the spectral abscissa and radius. Let us
consider the following spectral function
                                   def
                             γ(X) = max κ(λi (X))
                                         i

where κ : C → R is either the real part function or the modulus function
and consequently γ(X) = α(X) or γ(X) = ρ(X) depending on the instance we
consider.
   Let us further suppose that there is one and only one i which verifies

                               γ(X) = κ(λi (X)) .

In other words, there is only one active eigenvalue. In the following, we use the
notations λi = λi (X) when the context makes it possible.
    Following our assumptions, the directional derivative of γ(X) corresponds
to the directional derivative of (κ ◦ λi )(X) in the direction H. In virtue of the
chain rule, its expression is given by

                      Dγ(X)[H] = h ∂κ(λi)
                                    ∂λi , Dλi (X)[H]i ,                     (1.40)

where expressions for ∂κ(λ i)
                       ∂λi and Dλi (X)[H] are still needed. The expression of
∂κ(λi )
 ∂λi    depends on the actual form taken by κ(λ). In continuous-time we have
that,
                                  ∂κ(λi )
                                          =1.                               (1.41)
                                   ∂λi
If we consider the discrete-time case, then
                                 ∂κ(λi )    λi
                                         =       .                          (1.42)
                                  ∂λi      |λi |
     An expression for Dλi (X)[H] is in turn easily obtained from the definition of
eigenvalue. Suppose vi and ui are the left and right eigenvectors associated with
λi . Without loss of generality we can further assume that they are normalized
such that [50, Theorem 6.3.12]

                               kui k = 1 = vi∗ ui .

Then
                                  vi∗ Xui = λi ,
28                                                          Chapter 1. Preliminaries


and we get
                             Dλi (X)[H] = vi∗ Hui .                          (1.43)
    When λi is a simple active eigenvalue, the equations (1.41), (1.42) and
(1.43) can be plugged successively in the theoretic expression of the directional
derivative (1.40) to obtain the two expressions [20]

                  Dα(X)[H] = h∇α(X), Hi = hvi u∗i , Hi ,                     (1.44)
                  Dρ(X)[H] = h∇ρ(X), Hi = h |λλii | vi u∗i , Hi .            (1.45)

Directional derivatives of the root abscissa and radius. Directional
derivatives for the root abscissa and the root radius can be obtained likewise.
With the use of the same notations, a general expression for the directional
derivative of γ(x) is given by

                        Dγ(x)[h] = h ∂κ(λ i)
                                      ∂λi , Dλi (x)[h]i .                    (1.46)

The previous developments can be adopted without much change. Still one
must pay attention to the space in which one is working. When working with
a monic polynomial of degree n, x(λ) ∈ Cn+1 but there are only n degrees of
freedom such that the directional derivative is computed in a direction h ∈ Cn .
The problem is not encountered when working with companion matrices since
then the associated polynomial is always monic.
    The expressions for ∂κ(λ
                          ∂λi
                             i)
                                do not change. The only difference is found in
the expression of Dλi (x)[h]. Its expression can be found by writing the total
variation of the polynomial p(λ, ) obtained by perturbing x(λ) as follows :

                             p(λ, ) = (x + h)(λ),

where h ∈ Cn , khk = 1, is the direction in which we want to compute the
derivative and  > 0 is some small scalar increment. As λi is a root of x(λ), its
directional derivative must satisfy

                                 p(λi (), ) = 0 .

The total variation of this last equation takes the expression for some small
displacements δλi and δ,

                     ∂p(λi (), )       ∂p(λi (), )
                                   δλi +               δ = 0 ,
                        ∂λi                  ∂
which in turn implies
                                            
                     δλi    ∂p(λi (), )       ∂p(λi (), )
                         =−                                   .              (1.47)
                      δ        ∂                 ∂λi

An expression for the factors of the right-hand side in (1.47) is obtained easily.
We have
                            ∂p(λi (), )
                                          = hT πλn−1
                                  ∂              i

    Plugging these results in (1.47) and in turn in (1.46) along with the defini-
